notes:
All 315 names in batch6 (n 2100-2414) are mapped. Things to check:
(1) Victorian genera mean different birds today. Tringa/Tringæ = modern Calidris (Dunlin, Knot, stints). Totanus/Totani = modern Tringa (shanks), and could also cover Common Sandpiper. Turdus musicus = Song Thrush here, because iliacus is used for Redwing, even though Linnaeus's musicus was the Redwing.
(2) 'Turdidæ' and its OCR forms (Turdide, Turpipz, Torpip#, Twrdide) are mapped to family Turdidae. The Victorian family was broader (chats, Robin, redstarts, sometimes warblers). I read Turpipz/Torpip# as small-caps OCR of TURDIDÆ; check against the scans.
(3) 'Thrush'/'Thrushes' (1,248 observations) are mapped to Song Thrush as you said; rush-night plurals may lump other Turdus.
(4) 'Wild Duck' (117+82 observations) is left at family Anatidae, but where it is the committee's species heading it is Yarrell's Mallard. Only 'Wild-drake' is mapped to Mallard.
(5) Single-name puzzles needing the source: Titmouses 'build on the Rock'; White Owl (the Redcar 'great White Owl' is likely Snowy Owl, others Barn Owl); White/'Kittiwake variety' gulls (possibly Ivory Gull); Wilson's Petrel (likely misidentified unless at sea); White/Yellow-spotted Hawks; Whitebreast; Willy the Wisp; Winter Sparrows; 'Bass' Gulls; White-backed; white-bellied variety (Brent?); Welw Bail (Water Rail?); Wen (Wren?); Tick Terns; Yellow Shanked Sandpiper; the quoted 'Grey' Plover entries; Oct. 27th Wood Wren; Turdus varius three times in one October.
(6) 'Young Curlew' and 'Whimbrel, or young Curlew' are left at genus Numenius, because keepers called May Whimbrels 'young Curlews'.
(7) The U. alle/brunnichii/troile and Œdemia nigra examples may come from foreign (Faroe or Heligoland) lists. Check the locality before using them as British records.
(8) IOC names used: Western House Martin, Western Yellow Wagtail, Eurasian Whimbrel, Common Murre, Thick-billed Murre, Curruca communis, Zoothera aurea for White's Thrush. Pied and White Wagtail are both mapped to Motacilla alba.
